steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Every component has a standard symbol: resistor (zigzag or rectangle), capacitor (parallel lines), diode (triangle with bar), transistor (arrow on emitter).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Wires without a junction dot do not connect; wires that cross with a dot at the intersection are connected.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Draw circuit diagrams with the signal flowing from left to right and power rails at the top (positive) and bottom (0 V / ground).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Label all components with their values (e.g. R1 = 10 kΩ, C1 = 100 μF) and reference designators.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: How do you tell whether two crossing wires in a circuit diagram are connected? | Q: Why should circuit diagrams be drawn with signal flowing from left to right? | Q: What information should be labelled on each component in a circuit diagram?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: If there is a filled dot at the crossing point, the wires are connected; if there is no dot, they are not connected. | It follows standard convention, making the diagram easier to read and understand; input is on the left and output is on the right. | Each component should have a reference designator (e.g. R1, C1) and its value (e.g. 10 kΩ, 47 μF).

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: When drawing circuits, use a ruler and leave enough space between components for clear labels. Always include junction dots where wires connect; missing dots can make your diagram ambiguous. Label input and output terminals clearly, and show the power supply connections to ICs. When interpreting a circuit, break it into functional blocks (input, processing, output) to understand its overall purpose. Use the standard WJEC symbol set; do not invent your own symbols for components.
